title: Candidate prompt change displaced the intended editorial hierarchy and triggered a rollback
description: A single added section in the Narrative user prompt — intended to “Preserve Editorial Intent from the Synthesis” — produced consistent, repeatable degradations in both Narrative and Compose outputs: company-level identity and audience were subordinated while orchestration became central, unsupported claims appeared, and the change was not promoted. The production prompt was restored byte-for-byte.
audience: Prompt engineers, editorial leads, release managers
rationale: This experiment shows a straightforward operational risk: even a small, generic prompt change can reliably alter high-level emphasis and introduce editorial regressions that fail promotion gates. Teams deciding whether to change system prompts need evidence that a change preserves the intended hierarchy before promoting it.
evidence: Facts: the candidate prompt added one generic section titled “Preserve Editorial Intent from the Synthesis” and contained no Nuëyon-specific wording; three candidate Narrative runs scored mean 4.00/10 vs baseline mean 6.00/10; three candidate Compose runs scored mean 3.33/10 vs baseline mean 5.67/10; all candidate Narrative and Compose runs made orchestration central and introduced unsupported additions; decision: “Do not promote. Candidate was worse on mean score… failed the orchestration hierarchy and factual restraint gates in every run,” and production prompt was restored (byte-for-byte SHA match). Inference: the added prompt section correlated with the observed editorial drift and regressions. Unknowns: the exact causal mechanism inside the model that produced the drift (e.g., how the new phrasing interacted with the Synthesis content or model internals).

title: Factual/editorial restraint is a hard promotion gate and determined the outcome
description: The rubric explicitly treats factual/editorial restraint (no unsupported audience, need, benefit, capability, traction, launch status, or commitment) as a hard gate. Candidate outputs repeatedly failed this gate by introducing validation intent, audience labels, or implied commitments, and that failure alone was decisive for rejection.
audience: Release decision-makers, QA reviewers, product communications owners
rationale: When editorial fidelity is a requirement, an explicit hard gate for unsupported claims focuses reviews and makes promotion decisions binary rather than purely comparative. Communicating this helps teams understand which failure modes will block changes regardless of other improvements.
evidence: Facts: rubric criterion D measures factual/editorial restraint and is described as “a hard promotion gate”; the report states “No candidate run passed this gate. The Narrative outputs introduced validation intent/commitment, an audience of founders/product leaders/builders, or a need for coordinated AI. The Compose outputs repeated or extended those additions. This is a hard failure.” Inference: failing criterion D was sufficient to decide against promotion. Unknowns: whether remediation confined to removing specific unsupported claims would have sufficed, or if deeper prompt redesign was required.

title: A generic 'preserve editorial intent' rule without story-specific constraints proved insufficient
description: The candidate added a general-purpose instruction to preserve primary message, audience, and theme hierarchy, but it contained no story-specific wording. Despite that, the change did not prevent hierarchy drift and introduced new unsupported framing — suggesting that generic editorial-preservation language alone may not reliably enforce nuanced priorities for a particular story.
audience: Prompt writers, editorial policy designers, SREs for ML platforms
rationale: Many teams prefer reusable, generic guardrails in system prompts. This experiment provides a concrete counterexample: a generic guardrail can fail to preserve story-specific priorities, so teams should validate such rules against the exact content they will govern.
evidence: Facts: the added candidate section is described as generic and “contains no Nuëyon-specific wording or this story's details;” candidate runs consistently subordinated company identity and made orchestration central; the analysis concludes “the candidate prompt was not sufficient to protect the supplied editorial intent.” Inference: the generic phrasing likely lacked specificity needed to keep the intended emphasis. Unknowns: whether a more specific preservation instruction (e.g., explicit weightings or examples) would have succeeded, or whether the failure arose from interactions with the existing Synthesis text.

title: The experiment process was rigorous and reproducible, but has measurable limitations
description: The run used explicit commit hashes, SHA-256 checks, saved baseline/candidate outputs, three runs per condition, and full build/test/rollback verification; yet it also documents limitations (no seed/temperature control, possible backend model changes, and limited statistical significance).
audience: Engineering managers, experiment designers, compliance/ops teams
rationale: Documenting both strong controls and explicit limits helps readers judge how much confidence to place in the result and what follow-up experiments or mitigations are required before broader conclusions are drawn.
evidence: Facts: repository, branch, and commit are recorded; baseline and candidate prompt files and diffs are saved; baseline user prompt SHA-256 and other hashes are provided; three runs per condition were executed with identical workflow and model alias gpt-5-mini; full console logs and outputs were archived; production prompt was restored and builds/tests passed (165 tests passed). Limitations listed: no seed/temperature override, three runs not statistically significant, model alias backend may change. Inference: the experiment is methodical and well-documented but not conclusive at statistical significance. Unknowns: whether re-running with controlled seeds or more runs would change the outcome, or whether a different model backend would behave differently.
